title: Colonialism and Modern Income: Islands as Natural Experiments
research_question: Does the length and nature of European colonial rule causally affect the long-run economic prosperity of formerly colonized territories? Specifically, how do the duration of colonization, the identity of the colonizing power, and the historical era of colonization shape modern income per capita and infant mortality?
data_description: The authors construct a new database of 81 islands in the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans, drawing on a UN islands database supplemented with national statistical agencies, the Asian Development Bank, Encyclopedia Britannica, the Pacific Islands Yearbook, and individual island histories. For each island they record GDP per capita in 2000 (from UN figures or island-level statistics), infant mortality in 2002, island area, latitude, population, and a detailed colonial history including first European sighting, first and last years as a colony, and identity of colonizing power (Britain, France, Netherlands, Germany, Spain, Portugal, Japan, or the United States). Wind data — monthly average east-west and north-south wind vectors and their standard deviations on a one-degree grid — come from CERSAT satellite measurements. Sample selection restricts to islands requiring open-ocean sailing from Europe and under 150,000 sq km. The unit of observation is an individual island.
institutional_context: During the Age of Sail (roughly 1500-1900), European powers discovered and colonized hundreds of oceanic islands. Which islands were found, revisited, and settled depended heavily on prevailing wind speed and direction, since sailing ships could only sail about twenty degrees into the wind and longitude could not be precisely measured before the mid-eighteenth century, making latitude sailing along consistent downwind corridors the dominant navigation method. Many discoveries were highly idiosyncratic — products of mutinies, shipwrecks, and accidental encounters. Colonial experiences varied widely: Spanish encomienda-style rule and early sugar-slave economies in the Atlantic differed sharply from later Pacific colonization involving missionaries and small administrative posts. Islands also varied in colonizer identity, era of colonization (pre- versus post-Enlightenment), and whether colonial status persisted into 2000. With the advent of steamships in the early twentieth century, wind ceased to matter for transoceanic travel, severing its link to contemporary economic activity.
